title: Tradeshow playbook: how Jason Cohen ran booths at dozens of shows
summary: A practical checklist from running dozens of tradeshow booths at Smart Bear. Covers setting a goal, presenting, booking meetings with press and customers, using the booth as live market research and pitch testing, and following up afterward.

principles.text: Set one primary goal for each tradeshow so you can decide and judge success.
principles.quote: A goal helps you make the decisions below and provides a yardstick for whether the tradeshow was "successful," and therefore whether you should do more.

principles.text: Always give a vendor presentation; depth with 20 people beats seconds with hundreds at the booth.
principles.quote: Even if just 20 people come to your talk, that's 20 people you get to talk to in depth for 45 minutes--far more valuable than talking to 100 of people at your booth for 5-60 seconds.

principles.text: Book meetings before the show, especially with editors, bloggers, customers and partners.
principles.quote: I've been published in every major programming magazine; almost all of that I can directly attribute to talking with editors at tradeshows!

principles.text: Treat the booth as an A/B test of your pitch, then move the winner to your home page.
principles.quote: A tradeshow is a wonderful place to test attention-grabbers. What gets people to stop? To laugh? To say "OK, fair enough, tell me more?"

principles.text: Ask questions instead of pitching; curiosity earns you permission to sell and doubles as market research.
principles.quote: If you start chatting they will actually ask you for a pitch as a form of reciprocation. Then you've got permission to "sell," and they're truly listening.

principles.text: Follow up after the show; people forget you within days, so quality beats swag volume.
principles.quote: Attendees are saturated with presentations and vendor pitches, so there's a 99% chance they've forgotten about you.
